story.text: Elinor Ostrom asked why some commons last for centuries while others collapse in a generation. Her answer was eight design principles: patterns that long-lasting commons share. Most of them are about the rules a group makes for itself. So if a group's agreements are coded with Ostrom's own grammar, part of the answer to "will this commons last?" can be read straight from the coding.

This page sets out the idea and its limits. The crosswalk itself is on [[Ostrom Design Principles And Agreement Coding]]. A first try, on a real-looking garden bylaw, is on [[Garden Bylaw Viability Profile]].
## The coding

Every agreement sentence answers a small set of questions. A rule about what people do answers WHEN?, WHO?, MUST, MAY, OR MUST NOT?, DO WHAT?, TO WHAT?, HOW?, and OR ELSE?. A creating agreement, which makes a role, group, or thing, answers WHAT ARE WE CREATING?, MUST OR MAY?, FORMED?, and OUT OF WHAT?. These are Ostrom's Institutional Grammar (IG 2.0) in plain words, and the Agreement Checker fills them in from ordinary sentences.

Once an agreement is coded, its answers can be searched. Is there any sentence whose action is "monitor" or "inspect"? Does any OR ELSE step up for a second offence? Who MAY change the rules, and are the people affected among them? Each of these is a design principle, asked of the coding.
## What the coding can show

Seven of the eleven design principles leave a clear trace in an agreement's text: boundaries, the people affected making the rules, monitoring of users and of the resource, graduated sanctions, and a way to resolve conflict. Three leave a partial trace. One, whether the rules fit local conditions, cannot be read from the text at all.

The coding can also sort every sentence by Ostrom's levels of action. Operational rules are about doing the work: water, pay, harvest. Collective-choice rules are about making and changing those rules: amend, vote, decide. Constitutional rules are about how the rule-makers are chosen and how they decide. A commons with operational rules and nothing above them can follow its rules but cannot change them, and that shows plainly in the coding.

A second sort uses Ostrom's seven rule types: boundary, position, choice, aggregation, information, payoff, and scope. Each rule's action says which type it is. The NDC School page [[Seven Questions]] puts these types in plain words.
## What the coding cannot show

The coding records the rules on paper. A commons lives or dies by the rules people actually use. Ostrom's own fieldwork showed written rules ignored and unwritten rules obeyed, again and again. So a profile built from coding is a structural screen. It can say "these rules have no monitoring in them." It cannot say whether anyone watches the water.

The evidence of use has to come from somewhere else: what people do, measured over time with SPC charts, asked in surveys such as the protection survey, or seen at the site. The most useful picture puts the two side by side, on paper and in use, principle by principle.
## How a profile should read

The output is a profile with one line per design principle. The lines are not added up into a score. Each line says one of four things: present, partial, absent, or can't tell from the text. Each says why, in plain words, and points to the sentences it read.

The design principles go with commons that last; they do not guarantee it. A profile with every line present is a good sign. It does not promise the commons will last. A profile with gaps is a list of conversations the group has not had yet.

The coding is only as good as the coder. The Agreement Checker's guesses are heuristic, and the group's corrections are what make the data trustworthy. Coding done by the people who live under the rules is slower and better.
## What it would take

One coding schema shared by every RCN tool: the Graph Tool, the database behind it, FedWiki pages, and the Agreement Checker. Then any agreement written anywhere carries its coding with it. A proposal is on [[Shared Shape For Coded Agreements]].
A viability lens that reads that coding and writes the profile in plain words, for example: "Nobody affected can change these rules."
Evidence from practice beside it, so a group sees what it wrote and what it does on the same page.
*Marc Pierson and Claude Opus 5.5 · October 2026*

story.text: For each of Ostrom's design principles: what it means in plain words, what in an agreement's coding counts as evidence, the question the Agreement Checker would ask, and what has to come from practice instead. The idea behind this page is on [[Commons Viability From Agreement Coding]]. A first try on a garden bylaw is on [[Garden Bylaw Viability Profile]].
The numbering follows Ostrom (1990) as refined by Cox, Arnold and Villamayor Tomás (2010), who split principles 1, 2 and 4 in two.
## At a glance

PrinciplePlain wordsReadable from the text?
1A User boundariesEveryone knows who is inYes
1B Resource boundariesEveryone knows what the shared thing isYes
2A Fit with local conditionsThe rules suit this placeNo
2B Costs in proportion to benefitsWhat you put in matches what you takePartly
3 Collective choiceThe people affected help make the rulesYes
4A Monitoring usersSomeone watches how the rules are kept, and answers to the usersYes
4B Monitoring the resourceSomeone watches the shared thing itselfYes
5 Graduated sanctionsConsequences start small and growYes
6 Conflict resolutionThere is a cheap, local way to settle disputesYes
7 Recognition of rightsOutside authorities let the group make its own rulesPartly
8 Nested enterprisesLarger systems are built of smaller self-governing onesPartly
## 1A · User boundaries
Plain words: everyone knows who is in and who is out.

Evidence in the coding: a creating agreement whose WHAT ARE WE CREATING? names the members, and whose FORMED? and OUT OF WHAT? say how someone becomes one. "Anyone who holds a plot counts as a gardener." Also rules whose WHO is a defined group rather than "anyone".
The checker asks: "This assumes everyone knows who counts as a gardener. Nothing here says." It already asks this today.
From practice: whether people outside the boundary actually stay out.
## 1B · Resource boundaries
Plain words: everyone knows what the shared thing is and where it ends.

Evidence in the coding: a creating agreement that defines the resource: the tank, the plots, the fishing grounds, the shared fund. Also TO WHAT? answers in the rules that point at a defined thing rather than a vague one.
The checker would ask: "These rules are about the water, but nothing says what the shared water is. Which tank, which taps?"
From practice: whether the boundary on paper matches the boundary on the ground.
## 2A · Fit with local conditions
Plain words: the rules suit this place, this resource, and these people.
Evidence in the coding: none that can be trusted. The text can mention local things, but whether the rules fit is a judgment about the place.
The checker would ask nothing. The profile says "can't tell from the text."
From practice: everything. Ask the people who live under the rules, and watch the resource over time.
## 2B · Costs in proportion to benefits
Plain words: what each person puts in matches what they take out.

Evidence in the coding: pairs of sentences. A permission or benefit, "Gardeners may water on their assigned days", matched by a duty with the same WHO, "Gardeners must give four work hours a season." Proportion shows when the duty scales with the benefit: hours per plot, dues per share.
The checker would ask: "Gardeners get water, but no sentence asks anything of them in return. Is that the agreement?"
From practice: whether the contributions are actually made, and whether people think the balance is fair.
## 3 · Collective choice
Plain words: the people affected by the rules help make and change them.

Evidence in the coding: collective-choice rules, whose DO WHAT? is amend, vote, decide, propose, or choose, and whose WHO includes the people the operational rules apply to. "Gardeners may propose a change to these rules at the spring meeting." "A change passes when two thirds of gardeners present agree."
The checker would ask: "Nothing here says how these rules can be changed, or by whom."
From practice: whether people affected actually take part, and whether changes they ask for happen.
## 4A · Monitoring users
Plain words: someone watches whether the rules are kept, and that someone answers to the users.

Evidence in the coding: a duty whose DO WHAT? is monitor, check, inspect, record, or report, held by a role. Then a creating agreement for that role whose OUT OF WHAT? is the users themselves, or a rule that the role reports to them.
The checker would ask: "The water keeper suspends watering for rule breakers, but no sentence says anyone watches for them, or who the keeper reports to."
From practice: whether the watching happens, and whether it is trusted.
## 4B · Monitoring the resource
Plain words: someone watches the condition of the shared thing itself.
Evidence in the coding: a duty to measure, read, or record the resource, held by a role. Also triggers: a WHEN? such as "when the tank is below half" assumes someone reads the tank.
The checker would ask: "This rule switches on when the tank is below half. Who reads the tank, and how does everyone find out?"
From practice: the measurements themselves, kept over time. This is where SPC charts belong.
## 5 · Graduated sanctions
Plain words: consequences start small and grow with how serious or repeated the breach is.

Evidence in the coding: several OR ELSE sentences for the same rule, with WHEN? answers that step up: "for a first breach, a warning"; "for a second, one week without watering"; "for a third, the plot is reassigned."
The checker would ask: "Every breach gets the same consequence. Does a first slip get the same as a third?"
From practice: whether the consequences are applied, and applied evenly.
## 6 · Conflict resolution
Plain words: there is a cheap, quick, local way to settle disputes, including disputes about the rules.
Evidence in the coding: a creating agreement for a venue (a mediator, a meeting, a council) and a rule that says who MAY bring a dispute to it and when.
The checker would ask: "If a gardener thinks a suspension was unfair, where do they take it?"
From practice: whether disputes get taken there, and settled.
## 7 · Recognition of rights
Plain words: governments and landowners outside the group respect the group's right to make its own rules.

Evidence in the coding: partial at best. A group's own text may name its lease, charter, or permit. The recognition itself lives in someone else's statements: the city's ordinance, the landowner's lease. Coding those outside statements too would make this readable.
The checker would ask: "These rules depend on the garden's right to the land. What gives the garden that right?"
From practice: whether outsiders override the group's rules, and how often.
## 8 · Nested enterprises
Plain words: when the commons is part of something larger, governance is layered, each layer self-governing and linked to the next.
Evidence in the coding: creating agreements that link the group to a larger body: "The garden sends one delegate to the neighborhood council." Also rules whose WHO is a body at another level.
The checker would ask, only when other levels exist: "These rules mention the neighborhood council. What links the garden to it?"
From practice: whether the layers actually talk to each other.
## Sorting by level

Every rule can also be sorted by what its action is about. Operational: doing the work. Collective choice: making or changing the operational rules. Constitutional: deciding who makes rules and how. A sentence's DO WHAT? usually tells which. A profile should report how many sentences sit at each level, because principle 3 depends on there being any collective-choice rules at all.
## Sources
Ostrom, Elinor (1990). Governing the Commons. Cambridge University Press.
Cox, Michael, Gwen Arnold and Sergio Villamayor Tomás (2010). A Review of Design Principles for Community-based Natural Resource Management. Ecology and Society 15(4): 38.
Crawford, Sue and Elinor Ostrom (1995). A Grammar of Institutions. American Political Science Review 89(3).
Frantz, Christopher and Saba Siddiki (2021). Institutional Grammar 2.0: A Specification for Encoding and Analyzing Institutional Design. Public Administration.
Ostrom, Elinor (2005). Understanding Institutional Diversity. Princeton University Press.
*Marc Pierson and Claude Opus 5.5 · October 2026*

story.text: A first try of [[Ostrom Design Principles And Agreement Coding]] on a real-looking agreement. The bylaw is the community-garden example used throughout the Agreement Checker, after the group has answered every question the checker asked. By the checker's own standards it is complete and clear. Read against Ostrom's design principles, it has more gaps than lines filled in.
## The bylaw

1. Gardeners must not water on days not assigned to them, unless hand-watering seedlings.
2. When the tank is below half, gardeners must not water their plots with sprinklers.
3. Gardeners may hand-water seedlings on any day.
4. The water keeper must suspend watering for one week for any gardener who breaks these rules.
5. Each spring, a water keeper must be chosen from the garden members.
6. Anyone who holds a plot counts as a gardener.
7. Each spring, the water keeper must assign watering days to every gardener.
## By level

Sentences 1, 2, 3, 4 and 7 are operational: they are about watering and about enforcing the watering rules. Sentences 5 and 6 create things: the water keeper and who counts as a gardener. No sentence says how any rule can be changed, or how the members decide anything together. The garden can follow its rules. On paper, it cannot change them.
## The profile
**1A User boundaries · partial.** Sentence 6 says who counts as a gardener: anyone who holds a plot. Nothing says how someone gets a plot or loses one, so the boundary has a door with no handle.
**1B Resource boundaries · absent.** The rules are about the water and the tank, but nothing says what the shared water is: which tank, which taps, whether rain barrels count.
**2A Fit with local conditions · can't tell from the text.** Ask the gardeners, and watch the tank through a dry summer.
**2B Costs in proportion to benefits · absent.** Gardeners get water. No sentence asks anything of them in return: no dues, no work hours, no share of filling or fixing the tank.
**3 Collective choice · absent.** Sentence 5 draws the keeper from the members, but does not say who chooses. Nothing says how the rules can be changed or who may propose a change.

**4A Monitoring users · partial.** The keeper suspends rule breakers, which assumes someone notices them. No sentence gives anyone the job of watching, and nothing says the keeper answers to the members.
**4B Monitoring the resource · absent.** Sentence 2 switches on "when the tank is below half". Nobody is named to read the tank or to tell the gardeners when it drops.
**5 Graduated sanctions · absent.** Every breach, first or fifth, gets the same week without water.
**6 Conflict resolution · absent.** A gardener who thinks a suspension was unfair has nowhere to take it.
**7 Recognition of rights · can't tell from the text.** The bylaw never says what gives the garden its right to the land or the water: a lease, a city program, a landowner's goodwill.
**8 Nested enterprises · not applicable yet.** The bylaw mentions no larger body. If the garden belongs to a neighborhood council or a city program, that link belongs here.
## What this shows

Of eleven lines, two are partial, six absent, two can't be told from the text, and one does not apply yet. None is fully present. Many gardens like this one run well for years on goodwill and unwritten habits, so this says nothing final about any real garden. It is a list of conversations this group has not had in writing yet.
Three of the gaps would be cheap to close. Who can change these rules, and how. Who reads the tank and tells everyone. Where a gardener takes a dispute.
## What the checker would need

Most of these lines need nothing the checker does not already collect. They need new questions asked of the same answers: does any DO WHAT? say amend, vote, or decide; does any DO WHAT? say monitor, read, or record; does any rule have more than one OR ELSE, stepping up. Lines 2A and 7 need evidence from outside the text, and the profile should say so plainly.
*Marc Pierson and Claude Opus 5.5 · October 2026*

story.text: A design note, for review before any code changes. It proposes one way to store an agreement coded with Ostrom's Institutional Grammar, used the same way by the Agreement Checker, the Graph Tool, FedWiki, and the database. The reason for wanting it is on [[Commons Viability From Agreement Coding]]. What it would let a group check is on [[Ostrom Design Principles And Agreement Coding]].
## Why one shape
Today each tool keeps the coding its own way. The checker holds it in the browser. The drawings keep it in node properties. FedWiki pages hold only the sentences. The database holds none of it.

Two of those ways would go wrong as soon as the coding travels. The Graph Composer treats nodes with the same kind and the same name as one thing, so every statement in a drawing would collapse into one. The database merges drawing nodes by kind alone, so "WHO?" and "GARDENERS" would become two wordings of one idea.

Both behaviours are right for what they were built for: drawings of ideas, where "Housing" in two drawings really is one idea. A coded agreement is different. Each sentence is one particular rule, adopted by one particular group, with its own parts. It needs to be stored as a record.
## The things
**Agreement.** One document a group adopted: a bylaw, a charter, a house agreement. It knows its title, where it lives (a FedWiki page or a file), when it was adopted, and which group adopted it.
**Statement.** One sentence of an agreement, with exactly one MUST, MAY, or MUST NOT, or one creating agreement. It carries:

- its own words, as the group wrote them
- its answers to the questions, as fields: WHEN?, WHO?, MUST, MAY, OR MUST NOT?, DO WHAT?, TO WHAT?, HOW?, OR ELSE? for a rule; WHAT ARE WE CREATING?, MUST OR MAY?, FORMED?, OUT OF WHAT? for a creating agreement
- its strength: agreed rule, shared expectation, shared habit, or creating agreement
- its level: operational, collective choice, or constitutional
- its rule type: boundary, position, choice, aggregation, information, payoff, or scope
- who coded it, and whether the group has checked the coding
- whether it is in force, proposed, or retired

**Role, group, or resource.** The people and things the statements are about: the water keeper (a role), gardeners (a group), the tank (a resource). These already exist in the database's Ostrom layer as positions, participants, and resources, so coded agreements use them rather than inventing new ones.

**Observation.** A piece of evidence about whether a statement is followed in practice: a log, a survey answer, an SPC chart, a signed badge, or someone's account. Each is marked observed or asserted, the same distinction the database already makes on every transaction.
## The links
A statement belongs to its agreement.
A rule's WHO points to a role or group. Its TO WHAT? points to a resource when there is one.
A creating agreement points to the role, group, or resource it creates.
A statement points to the statement that backs it: the red "backed by" line in the drawings. This is Ostrom's vertical nesting.
Statements joined by ALL OF THESE, ONE OR MORE, or EXACTLY ONE point to a join, which carries which of the three it is. This is Ostrom's horizontal nesting.
A statement points to the action situation it governs, in the database's existing Ostrom layer. That is what turns a situation's rule types from "unspecified" to "specified".
An observation points to the statement it is evidence about.

Two links are never stored, because they can always be worked out. The purple "defined by" line follows from a rule's WHO and the creating agreement that created it. The checker's "what does this rule assume already exists?" question is the same lookup, run the other way.
## Who is the same as whom
This is the part that fixes the collapse. Four rules:

1. **A statement is its own thing.** It is identified by its agreement plus a statement number that never changes, even when the wording is edited. Two statements are never merged, however alike their words.
2. **A part belongs to its statement.** "MUST NOT" in sentence 1 and "MUST NOT" in sentence 2 are two separate answers.
3. **Roles, groups, and resources are shared within a commons.** "Gardeners" in sentence 1 and "gardeners" in sentence 6 of the same garden are one group, so every rule about gardeners links to the same place. "Gardeners" in two different gardens are two groups. A link between them is made on purpose, for example when one garden belongs to a larger network.
4. **Ostrom's term says what kind of thing something is.** Attributes, Deontic, Constituted Entity: these classify. Identity comes from rules 1 to 3.

In the Graph Tool this means: each statement node and each answer node carries a name built from its agreement and statement number, so the Composer keeps them apart; role, group, and resource nodes carry their plain name, so they merge across sentences; and the question nodes in the teaching drawing stay unnamed, because they really are "the kind itself".
## One file, many views

The source of truth is a coded-agreement file, written by the Agreement Checker and kept beside the agreement itself. The drawing, the FedWiki page, and the database are all built from it. Nothing writes coding back from a drawing, because a drawing is where people move boxes around, and moving a box should never change what a rule says.
A sketch of the file, for the first garden sentence. The garden's name and date are made up:

```json
{
  "agreement": { "id": "garden-bylaw", "title": "Garden Bylaw", "commons": "Elm St Community Garden", "adopted": "2026-04-12" },
  "statements": [
    { "n": 1, "kind": "rule", "text": "Gardeners must not water on days not assigned to them, unless hand-watering seedlings.",
      "when": "unless hand-watering seedlings", "who": { "group": "gardeners" }, "deontic": "MUST NOT", "do": "water",
      "how": "on days not assigned to them", "backedBy": 4,
      "strength": "agreed rule", "level": "operational", "ruleType": "choice",
      "codedBy": "the checker, corrected by the group", "groupChecked": true, "status": "in force" }
  ],
  "roles": [ { "name": "water keeper", "createdBy": 5 } ],
  "groups": [ { "name": "gardeners", "createdBy": 6 } ],
  "resources": [ { "name": "the tank", "createdBy": null } ],
  "observations": []
}
```
The names in this file are the plain ones. Ostrom's terms are added when the file is read: "who" becomes Attributes, "do" becomes Aim, and so on, from one table kept in one place.
## How each tool carries it

**Agreement Checker.** It already keeps one record per sentence. It would add a stable statement number, the agreement's title and commons, and the list of roles, groups, and resources. Then it saves and opens coded-agreement files, besides making drawings.
**Graph Tool.** The drawings look the same. Their nodes gain the names from the identity rules, and each node records which statement and which question it comes from.

**FedWiki.** One page per agreement. Each sentence is its own story item, so it can be searched, linked, and forked. The coding travels with the page, first as a coded-agreement file attached to it, and later as its own item type, the way drawings travel as graph items today.

**The database.** A loader reads coded-agreement files into the Ostrom layer: agreements, statements, their links to roles, groups, resources and action situations, and observations. It keys statements by agreement and number, and roles, groups, and resources by commons and name. The idea-merging used for drawings is never applied to statements.
## What the viability profile then reads

Each design principle becomes a question asked of the stored statements. Principle 3, collective choice: is there any statement at the collective-choice level whose WHO includes the groups the operational rules apply to? Principle 5, graduated sanctions: does any rule have more than one statement backing it, stepping up? Principle 4B, monitoring the resource: does any WHEN? depend on a reading of a resource that no statement makes anyone responsible for?
This answers one of the database's own open questions. Design principles live as questions over the stored statements, so a group can see exactly which sentences each answer came from.
## Not settled here
The plain names for Ostrom's Conditions. WHEN? and HOW? are still stand-ins.
What to do when a WHO names two groups, such as "gardeners and volunteers": one statement pointing to two groups, or two statements.
What counts as an observation, and who may add one. This touches people's privacy and needs the same care as the Relationship Record: nothing about a person without that person.
Where coded-agreement files live: in the repository, as FedWiki assets, or both.
The richer levels of Ostrom's grammar, IG Extended and IG Logico, are left for later. This shape is IG Core.
## What would change

The Agreement Checker gains saving and opening coded-agreement files, statement numbers, and a commons name. The drawing export follows the identity rules. The teaching drawing gets names on its answer and statement nodes. A new loader brings coded agreements into the database's Ostrom layer. Nothing that already exists in the database changes, and no existing drawing is rewritten.
The suggested order: agree this note; then the file format and the checker; then the drawing names; then the loader; then the viability profile as questions over what is loaded.
*Marc Pierson and Claude Opus 5.5 · October 2026*
